1.0.s.en: (1) The growth of the children of Israel

1.0.0.en: The beginning of the Book of Exodus recalls what the Book of Genesis mentioned at its end (ch. 46): the children of Israel who entered the land of Egypt, seventy souls in number, including Jacob and his sons and grandsons who came from Canaan, in addition to Joseph and his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh (see the commentary on Gen 46:26). Note that they were few, merely a family, but God blessed it and it became a great nation.

1.1.0.en: Joseph and his brothers died. Joseph had represented the authority that protected and provided for his family, but in truth it was God who used Joseph. Even after his death, God blessed this family, so they multiplied greatly and became a large people, reaching about 2 million souls, at a time when the population of all Egypt was about 8 million; that is, they became about a quarter of the population of Egypt.

1.1.1.en: Joseph is a type of Christ: after Joseph's death the number of the children of Israel increased, and by the death of Christ He offered salvation to the many in the whole world who believed in Him.

1.1.2.en: Trust in God's blessing upon your life, however hard your circumstances may be and however those around you may have wronged you. He strengthens you and makes you grow until those who oppose you fear you, and He gives you grace and respect in the eyes of those around you.

1.2.s.en: (2) The forced labor and humiliation of the children of Israel

1.2.0.en: Many years passed after the death of Joseph, during which the Egyptians forgot his services or purposely disregarded them, because of their resentment toward the Hyksos who had ruled them in the days of Joseph, in addition to the nature of human beings, who do not preserve gratitude toward those who served them for a long time. A new king arose who did not care about Joseph and therefore did not care to honor his race, that is, the children of Israel.

1.3.0.en: Let us deal wisely with them: let us persecute them craftily.

1.3.1.en: Get them up out of the land: leave Egypt and return to Canaan, so that the Egyptians would lose this labor force that served them.

1.3.2.en: When this king noticed the tremendous increase of the children of Israel, he considered with his counselors how to stop their growth and weaken them, fearing two things:

1.3.3.en: 1- Their increase in number would make them a force that frightens the Egyptians, so that if enemies attacked them from the east, the children of Israel would join them, fight Egypt and occupy it.

1.3.4.en: 2- Their increase would make them a force that could not be controlled, so that the Egyptians would lose the labor of the children of Israel if they left them and went up to the land of Canaan, where they had been living.

1.4.0.en: Pithom and Raamses: two cities located near Tanis, that is, Zoan, the capital of Egypt at that time, whose site is now in the Sharqia governorate.

1.4.1.en: Taskmasters: Egyptian overseers to lead the children of Israel in their work.

1.4.2.en: The first attempt to weaken the children of Israel and reduce their number was to exhaust them by building cities to store grain, weapons and ammunition near the capital. They worked in forced labor, that is, they received no wages but only their food, and it may have been scanty food, in the hope that some of them would die of exhaustion.

1.5.0.en: They were grieved: they were afraid.

1.5.1.en: Despite the harsh treatment of the children of Israel, God gave them strength and they endured the toil; on the contrary, they reproduced and bore many children, so their strength increased.

1.5.2.en: God is stronger than all who oppose you, and He mocks them. He permits them to show all their evil toward you, but at the same time He blesses you in the time of affliction, so you become stronger than before, and your heart is filled with a peace that terrifies your enemies.

1.6.0.en: Because the Egyptians feared the children of Israel, they grew more severe in their treatment of them and exploited them in many exhausting works, the most important of which were:

1.7.0.en: The Hebrews: the descendants of Eber, who was one of the forefathers of Abraham (Gen 11:15); also, since Abraham, the forefather of the children of Israel, had crossed the River Euphrates into Canaan, his descendants are called Hebrews.

1.7.1.en: The number of Hebrew women giving birth was estimated at tens and even hundreds of thousands; some of them gave birth without anyone's help, while others needed the help of the midwife. There were two famous midwives who were considered the chiefs of the midwives who delivered the Hebrew women, and Pharaoh summoned these two to him.

1.8.0.en: The stools: in ancient times women gave birth sitting on special stools whose position helped in delivery.

1.8.1.en: The king commanded the two midwives, together with all the midwives who followed them, that when they delivered the Hebrew women, if the child was a son they should kill him, and if it was a daughter they should let her live; in this way the number of men among the children of Israel would diminish and their strength would gradually weaken.

1.9.0.en: Although the command came from the king, and although they knew that he sent out spies to make sure his orders were carried out, they feared God more than men, because of their association with the children of Israel, from whom they had learned the fear of God; so they did not kill any male child.

1.9.1.en: If pressures and temptations multiply upon you to break God's commandments, remember that He is the most important person in your life, so do not anger Him, and trust that when you fear Him He will remove from your heart every fear of all human beings, and will even bless you and protect you.

1.10.0.en: The king became very angry when he learned from his spies that the newborn male children had not been killed, and he summoned the two midwives and rebuked them for what had happened; perhaps he intended to kill them.

1.11.0.en: The two midwives answered the king and gave him a plausible reason for the existence of newborn Hebrew male children, namely that the Hebrew women were strong in health and gave birth before the midwife arrived. This is true in many cases, but of course not in all cases, so this is considered a partial lie.

1.12.0.en: He made them houses: He gave them houses full of good things, and if they were not married, He granted them marriage and happy houses.

1.12.1.en: Although the two midwives had lied in part, God forgave them and blessed them because they feared Him, and He blessed their two houses. At the same time the people of the children of Israel continued to increase and grow.

1.13.0.en: Since the king's attempt to kill the males at their birth by means of the midwives had failed, and perhaps he doubted their words but had no proof of it, he resorted to another scheme to weaken the children of Israel, for he gave an extremely cruel command: to throw the newborn male children into the River Nile. By this he would achieve two things:

1.13.1.en: 1- Gradually reducing the number of the men of the children of Israel, so that the people would be weakened.

1.13.2.en: 2- Pleasing the Nile, which they worshiped as a god, by offering it human sacrifices.

1.13.3.en: But God, who is able to do all things, can preserve His people, and He made the child whom He wanted to live, namely Moses, be drawn out of the water and be brought up in the house of Pharaoh himself, so that he might lead his people and bring them out by the power of God in spite of the king.

1.13.4.en: Note: in ancient times the word Nile meant the River Nile and all its branches that go out from it and spread throughout the land of Egypt.

1.13.5.en: The birth of Moses, his upbringing and his flight to the wilderness

2.0.0.en: While the children of Israel were suffering from the king's cruel command to throw the newborn males into the Nile, a man of the tribe of Levi, Amram, married his father's sister, whose name was Jochebed (this was permitted before the giving of the Law through Moses), and they bore a handsome male child. His mother's heart was attached to him, and she believed in God, who is able to keep him safe (Heb 11:23), so she hid him in her house for three months, exposing herself and her family to being killed by the soldiers who went about the streets to listen for the voices of children and to learn the news of any pregnant woman when she gave birth.

2.1.0.en: An ark: a basket (a plaited basket). Bulrushes: a plant with broad leaves.

2.1.1.en: Slime: a kind of pitch (mineral pitch) that helps the bulrush leaves hold together and stick to one another. Flags: a plant with broad leaves that grows on the banks of rivers.

2.1.2.en: The three-month-old child grew bigger and the sound of his crying rose, so his parents were afraid and were compelled to prepare an ark of bulrush leaves and daub it with slime and pitch to make it a strong ark, and they put the child in it. His sister Miriam, who was thirteen years old, carried him and went with him to the River Nile and placed him on its surface among the flags, and she stood watching where the water would carry the ark. Perhaps her prayers mingled with her tears, like her parents, who had hope that God would save him, and so they did not throw him into the river but put him in an ark.

2.1.3.en: However hard the affliction is, lift up your prayers and do what is in your hand to do, even if it is small, like preparing this ark, and your God, who is able to do all things, can save you, because your prayers are very precious to Him.

2.2.s.en: (2) Moses is drawn out of the river

2.2.0.en: The Egyptian women believed that bathing in the water of the Nile had blessings, and some places in the Nile were set apart for the bathing of great ladies. So one of the princesses, that is, the daughter of Pharaoh, went down to bathe in the Nile with her maidens, and as she was bathing she saw an ark floating on the surface of the water. This was the ark that Miriam had placed, with her brother the child in it. She commanded one of her maids to bring it, and she marveled when she saw a child in it, and said that he must be one of the children of the Hebrews, who throw their male children into the Nile according to her father's command.

2.3.0.en: Miriam came near the place of the princess to hear what would happen to her brother, and she heard the princess declaring her admiration for the child and her wish to take him for herself and bring him up as her son. At this point God guided Miriam to go forward to the princess and ask her whether she wanted a nurse for the child.

2.4.0.en: The princess agreed to bring a Hebrew nurse, that is, a mother who had recently given birth to a child, so Miriam went with great joy, told her mother what had happened, and quickly brought her to the princess.

2.5.0.en: The princess commanded Jochebed, the mother of Moses, to nurse the child in her house and take care of him until he grew and she weaned him, and she promised her suitable wages. This was a declaration of the princess's adoption of Moses, so he became a grandson of Pharaoh.

2.5.1.en: Do not fear the threats of the wicked, for God saves you from their hands and even subjects them to you, as He subdued Pharaoh through his daughter, saving his son Moses and even paying the expenses of his living while he was in his house with his father and mother.

2.6.0.en: After the child was weaned, that is, after about two or at most three years, Jochebed brought her son the child to the princess, and she took him as her son by adoption and called his name "Moses", which means drawn out of the water. Jochebed took advantage of the opportunity of having the child with her in the house, and taught him all the spiritual teachings she could; perhaps she also visited him in Pharaoh's palace and was alone with him, as his nurse, to complete his spiritual teaching and fill him with her love.

2.6.1.en: Take care to teach your children even at a very young age, for they pick up everything that happens around them, even if they are only a few months old. The sight of you praying at home or reading the Holy Bible, or the sight of the prayers in the church ... affects them greatly and is imprinted within them, so that time cannot erase it.

2.7.s.en: (3) Moses tries to save his people by his own strength

2.7.0.en: Moses was brought up as a son of Pharaoh in the royal palace for 40 years, during which he learned the greatest sciences of the world, and they cared for his health and physical strength (Acts 7:22-23). His heart was attached to his God and to his people, who were humiliated at the hands of the Egyptians, and he thought of saving them, but unfortunately he relied on his own strength and not on God. As he was walking in the streets of the city, he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his brethren, and humiliating him; he became very angry and had pity on his wronged Hebrew brother, and thought of saving him and delivering him from this humiliation.

2.8.0.en: Moses relied only on his own strength and not on God, and therefore he was afraid ... so he looked this way and that way to make sure that no one saw him, then he fell upon the Egyptian and killed him and buried him in the ground (covered him over), and rescued his Hebrew brother.

2.8.1.en: The remedy for violence is not violence, nor resisting evil with evil. Ask God to give you wisdom to help others in a sound way, and know that if you become angry and resist evil with evil you will lose your peace and cause those around you to stumble, and you will not stop the one who wronged you from his evil, but will provoke him to wrong you again in a new way. The only one who benefits from all this is Satan, while God, the angels and the saints look at you with sorrow.

2.9.0.en: The next day Moses continued his attempts to save his people. As he was walking in the streets of the city he saw a Hebrew wronging a Hebrew, one of his brethren, so he reproved the wrongdoer and rebuked him so that he would not wrong his brother.

2.10.0.en: Moses was surprised that the wrongdoing Hebrew answered him violently and exposed to him what he had done in secret the day before, namely killing the Egyptian, so Moses knew that his secret had been discovered; that is, the Hebrew whom he had rescued the day before had told his loved ones, and what had happened spread among the Jews and then among the Egyptians. The wrongdoer denounced Moses' interference because he was not responsible for settling disputes like the judges, and then accused him of intending to kill him, although Moses had no such intention but was seeking peace and reconciliation among his Hebrew brethren.

2.11.0.en: The land of Midian: a region lying from the east of the Gulf of Aqaba to the middle of Sinai (Map 1). It was called this after Midian the son of Abraham by Keturah (Gen 25).

2.11.1.en: The news of Moses' killing of the Egyptian reached Pharaoh, and he knew that Moses' allegiance was not to him as his father and the one who raised him, but to his Hebrew race, so he commanded that he be arrested and put to death, because he represented a leader of a Hebrew revolt against the Egyptians. When Moses learned of this, he fled very far, from the east of the Delta to the east of Sinai and beyond, which is the land of Midian, and he came to a well, drank, and sat down to rest.

2.11.2.en: Success built on pride is quickly exposed to ruin, whatever its methods, so be humble and seek God's help before every work.

2.12.0.en: The troughs: basins beside the well that are filled with water for the animals to drink from.

2.12.1.en: In Midian there was a priest called Reuel, which means (God is a friend) (Num 10:29), and his title was Jethro, which means (the exalted or the preferred) (Ex 3:1). He had seven daughters who tended his sheep, and they came as they did every day to water the flock from the well; they drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's sheep.

2.13.0.en: Some shepherds came to water their flocks, and when they saw the troughs that the daughters of Reuel had filled, they took advantage of the women's weakness and drove them away. Moses was troubled by this injustice, so he stood up against the shepherds and drove them off, and the daughters of Jethro watered their flock. It appears from the verse that this injustice befell them every day, so that they were late in watering their flock. Here Moses' courage, justice and fairness to the wronged are evident, even toward those who had no relation to him.

2.13.1.en: Defend the wronged as much as you can, and wrong no one, but think of the good of others before your own good, for love does not seek its own.

2.14.0.en: Because of Moses' help to the young women, they hurried to water their flock, and their father Reuel was surprised at their quick return home. They told their father of Moses' help to them in drawing water and watering the flock, and they knew that he was an Egyptian man, perhaps from his clothes and his language.

2.15.0.en: Reuel invited Moses to eat a meal with him and welcomed him, and he sensed his chivalry, strength and love; likewise Moses felt at ease in his company and hospitality.

2.16.0.en: Zipporah: that is, a little bird.

2.16.1.en: Because the priest of Midian admired Moses, he welcomed him to dwell with him, and Moses also rejoiced to stay with him because of his balance and love, and he even began to help him in tending his flock. When love grew firm between them, and Moses admired one of his daughters, Zipporah, he married her.

2.17.0.en: Moses had a son whom he named Gershom, which means a stranger, to declare not only his being a stranger in the land of Midian, far from his Hebrew people, but also his being a stranger to the world as a heavenly man. Later another son was born whom he named Eliezer (ch. 18:2-4).

2.18.0.en: The Egyptians continued to humiliate the children of Israel until the king of Egypt died, who, it seems, had humiliated the children of Israel more severely than others, so they cried out to God to save them from this humiliation, whether by a new merciful king or by any other way.

2.19.0.en: And God remembered: not because God had forgotten, but He announces the time for fulfilling the promises.

2.19.1.en: God heard the cry of His people who were humiliated in Egypt and moved to fulfill His promises to His beloved ones, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the forefathers of this people, so that He would save them by His divine power, bring them back to the land of Canaan and give it to them as an inheritance.

2.19.2.en: God notices, and even suffers with you, in everything you endure, and He is ready to save you and support you if you cry to Him and persist in asking. So trust that you will receive mercy and help and experience His fellowship and power, however long the answer is delayed.
